title: Head movement allocation in freely-moving macaques learning object-context sequences
authors: Rahman, K. F.; Abbaspoor, S.; Zinke, W.; Tamaki, H.; Hoffman, K. L.
abstract: Flexible learning and long-term memory are hallmark features of primate cognition that are shaped by interactions with changing environments. A comprehensive understanding of these brain-body-environment interactions requires minimal constraints on behavior, and environments rich with conditional cues that encourage diverse behavioral dynamics. In this study, we introduce a multi-level enclosure (Treehouse) that allows for independent control of spatially distributed touchscreens for studying cognition in freely moving macaques. To test flexible learning, two monkeys completed trials consisting of a regular sequence of conditional object choices (targets) across four distinct spatiotemporal contexts (screens). Both monkeys acquired numerous unique, conditional object-context sequences without detriment to new learning as memoranda accumulated. They also successfully recalled their correct choices after weeks without exposure. To assess how monkeys allocate movement during learning and memory-guided decision making, we tracked their head kinematics and used recurrent neural networks to decode different aspects of their engagement with the environment during the choice epoch of the task. One such model predicted the position of the object about to be touched, including on error trials, tracking overt gaze towards objects. Separate models decoded sequence corner, the ordinal step, and the individual screen stations the monkeys occupied, despite identical stimulus layouts and behavioral demands at each station. Head movements also showed efficiencies that the task did not require: under conditions of uncertainty, monkeys were biased in their initial search locations to the targets that were closest to reach, and across days they made smoother head movements as training progressed, with no change in accuracy. These results demonstrate the potential of immersive 3-D environments, in which body kinematics can shed light on animals' goals, and reveal that situated learning in primates can be rapid, capacious, durable, and flexible.

title: Naked antisense oligonucleotides access the cytosol during early endocytic trafficking
authors: Sitarska, E.; Saminathan, A.; Scanavachi, G.; Somerville, E.; Stock, P.; Shen, P.; Kahne, D.; Courtney, M. F.; Reid, D. A.; Danielsen, M. B.; Davidsen, F. K. N.; Jensen, K. J.; Bennett, F. C.; Kirchhausen, T.
abstract: Phosphorothioate-modified antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) enter cells, but their site of productive escape remains uncertain. We combined live-cell imaging and ratiometric pH measurements to follow a Malat1-targeting ASO internalized without a delivery vehicle. In U2OS cells, less than 4% of internalized ASO reached the nucleus under conditions that reduced Malat1 RNA by >90%. Most ASO accumulated in late endosomes, endolysosomes and lysosomes as foci and broadly distributed luminal signal. These compartments underwent neutralization without detectable membrane rupture or galectin-3 recruitment. ASO foci showed constrained motion, consistent with association with endolysosomal constituents. L-leucyl-L-leucine methyl ester-induced membrane damage or Calcium dependent lysosome exocytosis released dextran while retaining luminal ASO. Loss of the stress-granule scaffolding proteins G3BP1/2 modestly enhanced ASO activity without detectable endolysosomal damage. Tantalosin, a small molecule that perturbs endosomal recycling, redistributed the ESCRT-III protein IST1 to endosomes. It enhanced early escape of SYTOX Green and ASOs, detected by nuclear accumulation, and increased Malat1 knockdown, with cell-type-dependent responses. Tantalosin did not detectably increase nuclear ASO accumulation after sequestration in late compartments. These findings place productive ASO escape early in endocytic trafficking, most likely in early or recycling endosomes, before sequestration in largely nonproductive late compartments.

title: SMARTFlexDB: a paired apo-holo RNA structure database and analysis platform for RNA conformational flexibility and small-molecule recognition
authors: Jiang, S.; Wei, J.; Taghavi, A.; Seabra, G.; Childs-Disney, J. L.; Li, C.; Disney, M. D.; Li, Y.
abstract: RNA structures can undergo substantial conformational changes upon small-molecule binding, yet existing structural resources provide only static RNA-ligand snapshots without connecting ligand-bound (holo) RNA structures to corresponding ligand-free (apo) conformations. SMARTFlexDB is a curated database and analysis platform that uses paired apo-holo RNA structures to characterize conformational differences and RNA-small molecule recognition. Candidate pairs were identified from the Protein Data Bank by matching RNA chains with at least 90% sequence identity and coverage, and fully conserved binding pocket nucleotides. The current release contains 434 binding pockets from 266 holo structures, linked to 186 apo structures to yield 1187 pocket-level apo-holo pairs organized into 734 database entries, spanning 150 small molecules and 23 RNA functional classes. Each entry integrates RNA sequence and secondary-structure annotations, apo and holo three-dimensional structures, RNA-ligand atomic interactions, and quantitative descriptors of global and local conformational changes. An interactive web interface enables users to explore sequence alignments and structural overlays, compare secondary structures and RNA motifs, and upload paired apo-holo structures for customized analysis. By linking ligand-bound and ligand-free RNA structures, SMARTFlexDB provides a robust foundation for investigating RNA structural flexibility and supporting RNA-targeted small-molecule drug discovery. The database and analysis platform are available at https://aidd.rc.ufl.edu/app/smartflexdb/.

title: Bayesian model-based method for clustering gene expression time series with multiple replicates
authors: Nushi, E.; Douillard, F. P.; Selby, K.; Lindström, M.; Honkela, A.
abstract: Background: In this study, we introduce a Bayesian model-based method for clustering transcriptomics time series data with multiple replicates. This technique is based on sampling Gaussian processes (GPs) within an infinite mixture model from a Dirichlet process (DP). Our method uses multiple GP models to accommodate for multiple differently behaving experimental replicates within each cluster. We call it multiple models Dirichlet process Gaussian process (MMDPGP) mixture model. We compare our method with state-of-the-art model-based clustering approaches for handling gene expression time series with multiple replicates. Results: To demonstrate the accuracy of our method we use it to cluster synthetically generated data sets. The clusters produced by our method on the synthetic data had a significantly higher purity score compared to the state-of-the- art approaches. We also present a case study where all methods are applied for clustering RNA-Seq time series of Clostridium botulinum with three different experimental replicates. The results obtained from the gene enrichment analysis showed that the number of significantly enriched sets of genes is larger in the clusters produced by MMDPGP. Conclusions: By modelling each replicate with a separate GP, our method can use the natural variability between experimental replicates to learn more about the underlying biology.

title: Revisiting the role of cAMP in Drosophila aversive olfactory memory formation
authors: Abe, T.; Yamazaki, D.; Hiroi, M.; Ueoka, Y.; Maeyama, Y.; Tabata, T.
abstract: In aversive olfactory conditioning in Drosophila melanogaster, an odor (the conditioned stimulus, CS) is paired with an electric shock (the unconditioned stimulus, US). Rutabaga adenylyl cyclase, which synthesizes cAMP in Kenyon cells (KCs), has long been proposed to act as a coincidence detector, synergistically activated by calcium/calmodulin in response to odor-evoked KC activity and by Gs downstream of shock-evoked dopamine signaling. This framework implies that CS+ responsive KCs, which receive both CS and US signals, should be distinguishable from the remaining KCs by elevated cAMP levels, such that elevated cAMP would selectively mark these KCs for memory-related plasticity. However, our live imaging revealed that olfactory stimulation alone activates dopaminergic signaling and elevates cAMP broadly across KC axons, with only weak spatial correspondence to sparse local Ca2+ responses, such that CS+ responsive KCs could not be distinguished from the remaining KCs by bulk cAMP levels. This observation challenges a key prediction of the Rutabaga coincidence-detection model. Our findings instead suggest that cAMP concentrations do not selectively mark CS+ neurons. Rather, we propose that the compartmental population dynamics of cAMP across the {gamma} lobe represent a KC-intrinsic expression of valence, integrated across compartments from multiple dopaminergic inputs. Associative conditioning reshaped dopamine responses to the CS+ odor, with corresponding changes in this compartmental cAMP pattern. Simultaneous imaging of cAMP and acetylcholine (ACh) revealed that conditioning establishes an inverse relationship between this pattern and ACh release for the CS+ but not for the CS- odors; this relationship was absent in rutabaga mutants. Pharmacological elevation of cAMP suppressed ACh release from KCs. These findings suggest that cAMP-dependent suppression of ACh release from KCs may shift the valence of the CS+ odor toward a more aversive state in conditioned flies, thereby contributing to aversive olfactory memory formation.

title: K2P Channels Regulate Presynaptic Organisation through a Membrane Potential-Independent Mechanism
authors: Meng, J.; Ramakrishnan, N.; Li, Y.; Boulin, T.; Gao, S.; Zhen, M.; Beets, I.; Schafer, W. R.
abstract: Neuronal ion channels have well-established effects on synaptic plasticity, in many cases by influencing pathways that depend on membrane excitability. Here we find that a C. elegans two-pore domain potassium (K2P) channel, TWK-40, regulates presynaptic organisation through a membrane potential-independent mechanism. Instead, this mechanism depends on TWK-40's effects on intracellular potassium levels. Loss-of-function mutations in twk-40 lead to excessive presynaptic protein accumulation, while gain-of-function mutations lead to depleted presynaptic components and cause synaptic transmission deficits. These changes in presynaptic protein abundance are phenocopied by transporter mutations predicted to alter intracellular potassium homeostasis in the same direction as TWK-40 mutations, but not by sodium channel mutations that mimic its effects on membrane excitability. This indicates that cytoplasmic potassium promotes presynaptic assembly. This process depends on pyruvate kinase PYK-1, a potassium-sensitive enzyme, and three transcription factors. These findings establish a new pathway linking neuronal potassium homeostasis to the control of presynaptic organisation and synaptic function.

title: Human ribosomes interactions reveal the binding landscape of neomycin
authors: Wu, M.; Zhu, L.; Wu, K.; Jia, C.; Zhang, X.; Zhao, Z.; Liu, H.; Yi, C.; Sun, S.; Liu, K.; Zhang, Z.; Guo, L.; Hou, X.; Li, W.
abstract: Aminoglycosides such as neomycin are clinically limited by toxicity, commonly attributed to the inhibition of mitoribosomes. Here, we investigate this model by integrating Cryo-EM and functional assays to assess neomycin's binding landscape and functional consequences for human ribosomes. Cryo-EM reveals extensive multi-site binding of neomycin on both human mitochondrial and cytosolic ribosomes in vitro, including conserved regions of the decoding center. In contrast, ribosomes isolated from neomycin-treated cells show markedly different patterns, with no detectable neomycin density on the mitoribosomes and reduced occupancy at a subset of cytosolic ribosome sites. Functional assays indicate that neomycin remained active in cells, inducing widespread stop-codon readthrough while having minimal effects on global mitochondrial and cytosolic protein synthesis. Together, these findings highlight a disconnect between the structural binding landscape and ribosome-associated neomycin recovered following cellular exposure, while linking neomycin exposure to altered translational fidelity with minimal effects on global protein synthesis.

title: Expertise modifies neural responses to causal inference during language comprehension
abstract: Linguistic communication relies on shared common ground, yet different individuals in a community have specialized semantic knowledge. As a key example, physicians acquire rich knowledge about the causes of illness. An open question is whether such "causal expertise" influences the neural basis of language comprehension. Here we tested the hypothesis that when understanding everyday language like, "Holly used a grimy faucet during her overseas plane ride. Now she has the stomach flu," medical experts retrieve richer representations in semantic networks of the brain. Physicians (n=16) and age- and education-matched controls (n=16) undergoing fMRI read two-sentence vignettes that elicited implicit causal inferences about illness or object mechanics as well as control vignettes that did not elicit causal inferences. Vignettes were linguistically matched across conditions and were accessible to experts and non-experts alike. Across both groups, causal vignettes about illness engaged a temporoparietal semantic network previously implicated in thinking about animates, i.e., people and animals (precuneus and left temporoparietal junction), whereas causal vignettes about object mechanics engaged a semantic network associated with places and objects. Critically, physicians' responses in the animacy network were more robust and self-similar, suggesting the activation of richer semantic knowledge. Medical expertise effects were specific to biological inferences rather than mechanical or mental state inferences. By contrast, individually localized frontotemporal language and frontoparietal reasoning networks did not respond preferentially to causally connected sentences or show effects of expertise. Our findings suggest that causal expertise alters neural responses to causal inferences that unfold automatically during language comprehension.

title: A multimodal dataset of EEG, eye-tracking, and physiological signals during naturalistic smartphone interactions
authors: Mishra, P.; Gandhi, T. K.; Gandhi, S. R.
abstract: Smartphones have become pervasive tools for communication, information consumption, and digital interaction, yet the neurophysiological dynamics associated with naturalistic smartphone use remain insufficiently characterized. Here, we present a multimodal physiological dataset collected during ecologically valid smartphone interaction and a subsequent relaxation condition. Twenty-three participants engaged with their most frequently used smartphone application (primarily gaming or short form video) for ten minutes, followed by a five-minute passive viewing of a standardized nature video. Simultaneous recordings were obtained from electroencephalography (EEG; 64 channels), wearable eye-tracking, photoplethysmography (PPG), and galvanic skin response (GSR) sensors. Questionnaire-based assessments, including the smartphone addiction scale (SAS) and the mobile phone problematic use scale (MPPUS), are also collected to characterize individual differences in smartphone-related behavioral traits. All data streams are synchronized using transistor-transistor logic (TTL) trigger signals to ensure precise temporal alignment across modalities. The dataset is organized according to the Brain Imaging Data Structure (BIDS) specification and is publicly available on OpenNeuro (Accession Number: ds007537). This dataset enables the investigation of neural, ocular, and autonomic responses during smartphone interaction and supports multimodal analysis of diverse smartphone behaviors while preserving ecological validity.

title: Human single-neuron correlates of somatosensation
authors: Liu, B.; Bjanes, D.; She, L.; Pejsa, K.; Lee, B.; Liu, C. Y.; Andersen, R. A.
abstract: Understanding the neural correlates of consciousness poses a central challenge in neuroscience, with longstanding debate over which cortical areas underlie subjective sensory perception. In the tactile domain, posterior parietal cortex (PPC) and primary somatosensory cortex (S1) are candidate cortical substrates for neural correlates of consciousness due to their crucial roles in somatosensory processing. Yet whether and how these regions contribute to conscious tactile perception remains unclear. Here, to address this issue, we leveraged chronic intracortical recordings to simultaneously monitor large ensembles of single neurons in grasp related cortical areas from three participants with tetraplegia while natural vibrotactile stimuli were delivered to a sensate region of the upper limb. We demonstrate that an orchestration of neural activity emerged across the grasp-related parietal-frontal network at near-threshold perception. Within this distributed network, we then focused on PPC and S1. While S1 responses closely tracked the amplitude of the physical stimulus, PPC activity covaried more strongly with awareness and confidence. This single-neuron evidence reveals PPC and S1 have complementary neural codes with PPC transforming physical stimulation into conscious perception whereas S1 is more sensitive to stimulus amplitude.

title: The genetic architecture of human DNA methylome variation
authors: Liu, T.; Macias-Velasco, J. F.; Zhuo, X.; Lin, J.; Porubsky, D.; Zhang, W.; Li, D.; Tomlinson, C.; Belter, E. A.; Dong, Z.; Dong, S.; Human Pangenome Reference Consortium,  ; Eichler, E.; Wang, T.
abstract: Population DNA methylome analyses remain largely confined to reference-defined genomic space despite extensive human genetic diversity. A central challenge is therefore to define comparable methylation phenotypes across diverse genomes and map the genetic architecture of methylome variation. Here, using 460 haplotypes from the Human Pangenome Reference Consortium Release 2, we develop two complementary pangenome-based frameworks: one compares methylation within homologous regions while retaining haplotype-specific structural configuration and CpG content; the other represents CpG island (CGI) variation at homologous loci as sequence-resolved alleles. We identified 47,039 CGI alleles, including 8,040 absent from CHM13; 62% were attributable to structural variants and 31% to small variants. Through local genealogies, we reconstructed CGI gain, loss and turnover, revealing how present-day methylation differences align with CGI evolutionary trajectories. We found that genome-wide, methylation variability was buffered against genetic diversity across more than 90% of the genome, with exceptions at extreme nucleotide diversity and locally around structural variants. Our methylation framework enabled population-scale allele-aware methylation quantitative trait locus (mQTL) mapping into non-reference and structurally complex sequence, where mQTL-associated intervals were enriched. mQTLs linked methylation to transcriptomic phenotypes, population differentiation and complex traits, supporting 8% of population differentially methylated regions and colocalizing with more than half of genome-wide association study loci. Together, our study redefines human methylome analysis and our findings reveal a genome-wide architecture of genetic-epigenetic coupling, reshaping how methylation variation is interpreted across human development and disease.

title: Structure of influenza D virus NS1 reveals a novel Zn-binding site and ssRNA-binding activity
authors: Ye, K.; Guan, M.; Kim, A. S.; Miller, M. D.; Ma, R.; Hamor, C. W.; Wang, A.; Yuan, Z.; Le, B. T.; Briggs, J. M.; Wan, X.-f.; Tao, Y. J.
abstract: Influenza D virus (IDV) is an emerging pathogen associated with bovine respiratory disease and has potential for zoonotic transmission. Although nonstructural protein 1 (NS1) is a major virulence factor in influenza A and B viruses, the structure and function of IDV NS1 remain poorly defined. Here, we determined crystal structures of the IDV NS1 N-terminal RNA-binding domain (NTD) and C-terminal effector domain (CTD). The NTD retains the conserved homodimeric six-helix fold, whereas the CTD adopts a distinct architecture containing a novel Zn2+-binding site. IDV NS1 CTD preferentially binds single-stranded RNA, and mutagenesis identified lysine and arginine residues critical for this activity. Single-residue substitutions disrupting either the Zn2+-binding site or RNA-binding interface prevented recovery of infectious recombinant IDV. These findings reveal distinct structural and functional features of IDV NS1 and establish the importance of CTD integrity for viral replication. Conservation of key CTD residues in influenza C virus NS1 suggests shared structural features that distinguish influenza C and D virus NS1 proteins from their influenza A and B counterparts.

title: Dissection of the contribution of bushy cell delays to sound localization in juvenile and adult Mongolian gerbils
authors: Sierksma, M. C.; Borst, J. G. G.
abstract: Sound sources along the azimuth generate interaural time differences in arrival (ITDs) at the ears. According to Jeffress hypothesis, ITDs are detected by coincidence-sensitive neurons of the medial superior olive (MSO) for which a differential axonal delay from each ear to the MSO compensates for the ITDs. The origin and development of these delays remain poorly understood. To this end, we made recordings from bushy cells (BCs), which project to both MSOs, in adult and in 2-4-week-old Mongolian gerbils of either sex. First spike latency revealed a frequency-dependent delay likely originating in the cochlea. Latencies were markedly larger for pure tone stimulation than for complex sounds. Combined with our published recordings from the MSO, we observed a developmental decrease in most delays, including the contralateral BC-to-MSO axonal delay. Unexpectedly, the ipsilateral BC-to-MSO axonal delay did not decrease. Anatomical brainstem reconstructions revealed that the inter-MSO distance was stable whereas the cochlear nucleus-to-MSO distance increased during development. Together, this indicated an increase in axonal propagation velocity, particularly for the contralateral projection. The variability in the averaged firing onset between BCs was found to be as large as the variance in bITDs, suggesting that BCs with matching firing onset are selected to converge onto the same MSO neuron. Together, our results indicate that the developmental speedup of ear-to-MSO delays contributes greatly to bringing the bITDs within their ecological range, but that the difference in path length is not overcome, keeping the ITD tuning biased to contralateral sound sources.
